description_full: Teekay Tankers Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, provides marine transportation services to oil industries in Bermuda and internationally. The company operates in two segments: Tankers and Marine Servies. It offers voyage and time charter services; offshore ship-to-ship transfer of commodities primarily crude oil and refined oil products; and tanker commercial and technical management services. In addition, the company is involved in the vessels management, procurement, and equipment rental businesses. It serves energy and utility companies, oil traders, oil consumers and petroleum product producers, government agencies, and various other entities that depend upon marine transportation. The company was incorporated in 2007 and is based in Hamilton, Bermuda.

financial_summary: Teekay Tankers Ltd. is a mid-cap energy business with a $3.1B market cap on $952M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -4% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are expanding by +15.8pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 25% against a 8% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $116M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.87× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 20% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 3.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Piotroski score 3/9 — the fundamentals are deteriorating on multiple fronts
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Financial quality metrics lag Energy peers
The commodity cycle — revenue and free cash flow are ultimately hostage to a price the company does not set, and the long-run energy-transition arc adds a structural overhang.
ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

sect: Its 32% operating margin runs 17pp above the Energy median (16%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.98x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-25.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 76% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 19% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 0.72, it is more defensive than the market.
About $42.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 73% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 60% below its DCF fair value of $225, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 20%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $192 to $269 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Energy peers: cheaper on P/E 5.3 vs 13.6 and EV/EBITDA 2.6 vs 7.1, richer on P/FCF 26.8 vs 14.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 75% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 3.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 18.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $110 on average, 23% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 25% clears the cost of capital of 8.4% by 17pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.32).
It converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.1x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 19pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $808.1M.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.6% over 3 years, 1.4% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 47%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 25.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -19.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.2x depreciation (20.0% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.4% on average.
own: Insiders own 20.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 71%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $1.9M sold).
It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (1.1% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 2,130 employees, each generates about $447K of revenue, 0.2x the Energy median, and revenue has grown 12.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $54K of free cash flow per employee.
